operations.name: Differentiate
operations.icon: a row of short vertical bars with one bar twice as tall
operations.description: Make one thing win the viewer's attention over everything else in the picture.

operations.name: Group
operations.icon: three small shapes wrapped by one rounded outline
operations.description: Make separate parts read as a single unit instead of a scatter of pieces.

operations.name: Sequence
operations.icon: a curved arrow passing through three points
operations.description: Decide what the viewer looks at first, next and last.

operations.name: Infer
operations.icon: a dot, a plus sign, a dot, an equals sign and an empty circle
operations.description: Leave a gap or a puzzle that the viewer fills in with their own idea.

domains.name: Feature
domains.icon: a short strip of three swatches, dark to light
domains.description: The raw look of marks and surfaces: colour, light and dark, texture, size and shape.

domains.name: Grouping
domains.icon: three short bars tied together by one bracket
domains.description: How the eye decides which parts belong together and which stand apart.

domains.name: Space
domains.icon: a horizon line with two lines running to a vanishing point
domains.description: Where things sit in the frame and in depth: placement, cropping, focus and overlap.

domains.name: Social
domains.description: Signals we read from people: faces, eyes, gestures and body language.

domains.name: Semantic
domains.description: What the depicted things are and what they stand for.

domains.name: Cultural
domains.description: Shared references the viewer already knows: genres, famous images, reading habits and ways of making.

techniques.name: Chiaroscuro
techniques.icon: a circle half lit and half in deep shadow
techniques.description: Strong light against deep shadow, so forms carve out of the dark.
techniques.citation: Arnheim, Art and Visual Perception (1954; rev. 1974), chapter on light

techniques.name: Pop-out
techniques.icon: a grid of small circles with one small triangle
techniques.description: One item differs from all its neighbours in a single obvious way, so it is spotted instantly.
techniques.citation: Treisman & Gelade, "A feature-integration theory of attention", Cognitive Psychology (1980)

techniques.name: Saturation blocking
techniques.icon: a grey rectangle with one solid bright square inside
techniques.description: Keep one area in rich, vivid colour and mute or grey out everything around it.
techniques.citation: Itten, The Art of Color (1961), contrast of saturation

techniques.name: Simultaneous contrast
techniques.icon: two identical small squares sitting on a light and a dark field
techniques.description: Pick the surrounding colour so the subject's own colour looks brighter, deeper or more intense than it really is.
techniques.citation: Chevreul, The Principles of Harmony and Contrast of Colours (1839); Albers, Interaction of Color (1963)

techniques.name: Warm and cool split
techniques.icon: a square split diagonally into a warm half and a cool half
techniques.description: Give the subject warm colours and the surroundings cool ones, or the reverse, so they separate.
techniques.citation: Itten, The Art of Color (1961), contrast of warm and cool

techniques.name: Scale disparity
techniques.icon: a huge circle beside a tiny one
techniques.description: Show something far bigger or smaller than it should be next to what surrounds it.

techniques.name: Semantic contrast
techniques.icon: a soft cloud shape facing a hard-edged block
techniques.description: Put two things with opposite meanings side by side so the clash grabs attention and makes a point.
techniques.citation: Phillips & McQuarrie, "Beyond visual metaphor: A new typology of visual rhetoric in advertising", Marketing Theory (2004)

techniques.name: Common region
techniques.icon: three dots inside a rectangle, two dots outside it
techniques.description: Things inside the same box, panel or patch of background read as belonging together.
techniques.citation: Palmer, "Common region: A new principle of perceptual grouping", Cognitive Psychology (1992)

techniques.name: Good continuation
techniques.icon: a smooth S-curve made of small dots
techniques.description: Parts that line up along one smooth line or curve are seen as one flowing thing, and the eye rides along it.
techniques.citation: Wertheimer, "Untersuchungen zur Lehre von der Gestalt II", Psychologische Forschung (1923)

techniques.name: Symmetry
techniques.icon: two mirrored half-shapes on either side of a dashed vertical line
techniques.description: Mirror the two halves of the picture so the whole reads as one balanced, stable shape.
techniques.citation: Arnheim, Art and Visual Perception (1954; rev. 1974), chapter on balance

techniques.name: Face schema
techniques.icon: two dots over a short curve inside a plain rectangle
techniques.description: Arrange things so they read as a face, which people notice first and see as one whole.
techniques.citation: Morton & Johnson, "CONSPEC and CONLERN: A two-process theory of infant face recognition", Psychological Review (1991)

techniques.name: Size hierarchy
techniques.icon: three circles shrinking from large to small
techniques.description: Make the most important thing biggest and step the rest down in size, so they are read in that order.
techniques.citation: Lupton & Phillips, Graphic Design: The New Basics (2008), chapter on hierarchy

techniques.name: Temporal synthesis
techniques.icon: one figure repeated three times, fading from left to right
techniques.description: Pack several moments of an action into one image, so the viewer reads it as movement over time.
techniques.citation: Gombrich, "Moment and Movement in Art", Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes (1964)

techniques.name: Leading lines
techniques.icon: two lines converging on a small dot
techniques.description: Use roads, rails, edges or beams in the scene to steer the eye toward the subject.

techniques.name: Gaze cue
techniques.icon: an eye with a dotted line running to a small dot
techniques.description: Where a figure looks, the viewer looks too, so their eyeline points at what matters.
techniques.citation: Friesen & Kingstone, "The eyes have it! Reflexive orienting is triggered by nonpredictive gaze", Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (1998)

techniques.name: Closure
techniques.icon: four corner brackets that imply a square
techniques.description: Leave a shape incomplete and let the mind finish it, so broken pieces still read as one form.
techniques.citation: Wertheimer, "Untersuchungen zur Lehre von der Gestalt II", Psychologische Forschung (1923); Kanizsa, Organization in Vision (1979)

techniques.name: Forced perspective
techniques.icon: a small hand outline pinching a distant tall shape
techniques.description: Line up near and far things from one exact viewpoint so they seem to touch or swap sizes.

techniques.name: Caricatural exaggeration
techniques.icon: a head outline with one oversized nose
techniques.description: Push a person's or thing's most telling feature far past real proportions.
techniques.citation: Ramachandran & Hirstein, "The science of art", Journal of Consciousness Studies (1999)

techniques.name: Contextual metaphor
techniques.icon: a small square sitting inside a circle where something else belongs
techniques.description: Place an ordinary object where something else normally goes, so the setting makes you see it as that other thing.
techniques.citation: Forceville, Pictorial Metaphor in Advertising (1996); Lakoff & Johnson, Metaphors We Live By (1980)

techniques.name: Complementary pairing
techniques.icon: two half-circles of opposite hues touching
techniques.description: Set colours from opposite sides of the colour wheel against each other so both look stronger.
techniques.citation: Itten, The Art of Color (1961), complementary contrast

techniques.name: Rim light
techniques.icon: a dark circle with a thin bright arc on one edge
techniques.description: Light from behind draws a bright edge around the subject and lifts it off the background.
techniques.citation: Bordwell & Thompson, Film Art: An Introduction (1st ed. 1979), on backlighting in three-point lighting

techniques.name: Silhouette
techniques.icon: a solid black figure against a light rectangle
techniques.description: Show the subject as a flat dark shape against light, so its outline alone does the talking.

techniques.name: Texture against flat
techniques.icon: a cross-hatched circle on a plain field
techniques.description: Put one rough, detailed surface on a smooth, plain one so the texture jumps out.

techniques.name: Isolation in void
techniques.icon: one small dot in a wide empty rectangle
techniques.description: Surround a single subject with empty space so nothing competes with it.

techniques.name: Selective focus
techniques.icon: one sharp circle among blurred, fuzzy circles
techniques.description: Keep the subject sharp and let everything in front of or behind it go soft.
techniques.citation: Bordwell & Thompson, Film Art: An Introduction (1st ed. 1979), on depth of field and focus

techniques.name: Color blocking
techniques.icon: a rectangle divided into three flat colour fields
techniques.description: Build the picture from large flat fields of solid colour, so things that share a colour read together.
techniques.citation: Wertheimer, "Untersuchungen zur Lehre von der Gestalt II", Psychologische Forschung (1923), grouping by similarity

techniques.name: Figure-ground reversal
techniques.icon: a square half black and half white with one wavy edge shared by both shapes
techniques.description: Shape the empty space so it forms a second image, and the viewer flips between the two readings.
techniques.citation: Rubin, Synsoplevede Figurer (Visually Experienced Figures) (1915)

techniques.name: Proximity clustering
techniques.icon: two tight clusters of dots with a gap between them
techniques.description: Things placed close together read as one group, and gaps split them into separate groups.
techniques.citation: Wertheimer, "Untersuchungen zur Lehre von der Gestalt II", Psychologische Forschung (1923)

techniques.name: Anthropomorphism
techniques.icon: a simple box shape with two stick arms
techniques.description: Give an animal or object human feelings, poses or behaviour, so the viewer relates to it like a person.
techniques.citation: Epley, Waytz & Cacioppo, "On seeing human: A three-factor theory of anthropomorphism", Psychological Review (2007)

techniques.name: Semantic compounding
techniques.icon: a circle and a square fused into one shape
techniques.description: Fuse two different things into one hybrid object that carries both of their meanings at once.
techniques.citation: Forceville, Pictorial Metaphor in Advertising (1996), hybrid metaphor

techniques.name: Center placement
techniques.icon: a dot at the crossing of a rectangle's two diagonals
techniques.description: Put the subject dead centre, where the frame's balance points straight at it.
techniques.citation: Arnheim, The Power of the Center (1982)

techniques.name: Frame within a frame
techniques.icon: a small rectangle nested off-centre inside a larger one, with a dot inside it
techniques.description: Use a doorway, window, arch or gap in the scene to box in the subject.

techniques.name: Body vector
techniques.icon: a stick figure with an outstretched arm pointing right
techniques.description: Point arms, limbs and posture toward something so the body itself directs the eye.
techniques.citation: Zettl, Sight, Sound, Motion: Applied Media Aesthetics (1st ed. 1973), on index vectors

techniques.name: Reading path
techniques.icon: a zig-zag line linking four small boxes
techniques.description: Lay the parts out along a planned route, such as a Z or an S, so the eye travels through them in order.

techniques.name: Pattern break
techniques.icon: a row of identical squares with one turned on its corner
techniques.description: Set up a repeating pattern, then break it in one place so that spot draws the eye.
techniques.citation: von Restorff, "Über die Wirkung von Bereichsbildungen im Spurenfeld", Psychologische Forschung (1933)

techniques.name: Occlusion
techniques.icon: one circle partly hidden behind a square
techniques.description: Let one thing hide part of another, which sets up front and back and leaves the hidden part to imagination.
techniques.citation: Kanizsa, Organization in Vision (1979)

techniques.name: Crop at the edge
techniques.icon: a rectangle with a large circle cut off by its right edge
techniques.description: Cut the subject off at the border so the viewer imagines what continues outside the frame.
techniques.citation: Bordwell & Thompson, Film Art: An Introduction (1st ed. 1979), on offscreen space

techniques.name: Visual quotation
techniques.icon: a small framed rectangle between two quote-like brackets
techniques.description: Borrow the pose, layout or look of one specific well-known image so viewers recognise the reference.

techniques.name: Visible facture
techniques.icon: three loose diagonal brush strokes
techniques.description: Leave the brush strokes, pencil marks or traces of making in plain view, so the viewer feels the hand behind it.

techniques.name: Genre quotation
techniques.icon: a rectangle with a bold title band across its top
techniques.description: Dress the image in the familiar look of a whole genre so viewers bring that genre's mood and expectations with them.
techniques.citation: Bordwell & Thompson, Film Art: An Introduction (1st ed. 1979), on film genres

techniques.name: Form substitution
techniques.icon: a circle with an arrow pointing to an identically sized sphere-like shape
techniques.description: Replace an object with a different one of the same shape, so the swap creates a new meaning.
techniques.citation: Phillips & McQuarrie, "Beyond visual metaphor: A new typology of visual rhetoric in advertising", Marketing Theory (2004)

techniques.name: Set apart
techniques.icon: a tight cluster of dots with one dot far off to the side
techniques.description: Move one element away from a tight group, so the gap alone singles it out.
techniques.citation: Wertheimer, "Untersuchungen zur Lehre von der Gestalt II", Psychologische Forschung (1923), grouping by proximity

techniques.name: Direct address
techniques.icon: an eye seen straight on, looking out of the frame
techniques.description: Have the subject look straight out at the viewer, so the eye contact grabs and holds attention.
techniques.citation: Senju & Hasegawa, "Direct gaze captures visuospatial attention", Visual Cognition (2005)

techniques.name: Incongruous object
techniques.icon: a small fish shape sitting on a bookshelf of plain rectangles
techniques.description: Put one thing in the scene that plainly does not belong there, so the eye goes straight to it.
techniques.citation: Loftus & Mackworth, "Cognitive determinants of fixation location during picture viewing", Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance (1978)

techniques.name: Limited palette
techniques.icon: three swatches of close, related hues side by side
techniques.description: Paint the whole image from a few related colours, so every part feels like it belongs to the same picture.
techniques.citation: Itten, The Art of Color (1961), on colour harmony

techniques.name: Repoussoir
techniques.icon: a large dark shape at the bottom-left corner with a small bright dot beyond it
techniques.description: Put a large, darker shape at the near edge of the picture, so the eye is pushed past it into the scene.

techniques.name: Arrow cue
techniques.icon: a small arrow followed by the numbers 1, 2, 3
techniques.description: Use arrows, numbers or other learned signs to tell the viewer where to look next.
techniques.citation: Zettl, Sight, Sound, Motion: Applied Media Aesthetics (1st ed. 1973), on index vectors

techniques.name: Missing piece
techniques.icon: a row of four circles with an empty dotted gap where a fifth should be
techniques.description: Show a familiar set or row with one member gone, so the viewer notices the absence and asks why.

branchTechniques.rationale: Colours opposite on the wheel make each other look stronger, so the paired subject stands out.
Meanings that clash beside each other make the pairing impossible to overlook.
The setting reassigns what the object is, and the viewer has to work out the new reading.
The borrowed genre look brings its mood with it, and the viewer reads the image through that genre.
The lit subject wins against the dark; the lever is value.
One odd colour, shape or size among sameness is the plainest way to stand out.
The only vivid area grabs attention; the lever is colour intensity.
The surround is tuned so the subject's colour reads stronger than its neighbours.
Colour temperature splits the subject from its setting.
A bright edge peels the subject off the background.
A dark shape on light makes the outline the strongest thing in the frame.
Surface detail against plainness singles out the textured part.
A repeating group is set up so the one member that breaks it stands out.
Empty space around the subject removes every competitor.
Sharpness at one depth plane separates the subject from what is in front of and behind it.
The frame's centre is its strongest position, so whatever sits there dominates.
An inner frame boxes the subject off from the rest of the scene.
Viewers find faces before almost anything else, so a face-like arrangement wins attention.
Shared flat colour binds separate parts into one unit (grouping by similarity).
A shared box or background patch makes its contents one group.
Parts along one smooth path read as one continuous thing.
Mirrored halves read as one balanced whole rather than two sides.
Broken pieces are completed by the eye into a single form.
Nearness is the most basic signal that things belong together.
Scattered parts snap into one whole the moment they read as a face.
Figures turned and reaching toward each other read as one group or one exchange.
The eye lands on the brightest light first, then works out into the shadows.
Stepped sizes set the reading order from largest to smallest.
A smooth line of parts is followed from one end to the other.
Repeated stages of one action are read as a series, in order, like frames.
Lines through the scene carry the eye to a destination.
Viewers look where the figure looks, which hands the eye to the next element.
A pointing arm or leaning body sends the eye along its direction.
A Z or F route works because it follows the viewer's learned reading direction (left to right in many cultures).
What is left out is filled in by the viewer, so the viewer takes part in making the image.
The viewer has to work out the trick of near and far to get the joke.
The second image hides in the empty space and is found only by looking again.
What is hidden behind something is left for the viewer to imagine.
Whatever lies past the border is completed in the viewer's head.
A face hidden in an object rewards a second look and invites the viewer to read a character into it.
The exaggeration comments on character, and the viewer reads the comment.
The viewer reads feelings and intentions into something that is not human.
Beyond catching the eye, the clash of meanings asks the viewer to resolve it into a message.
An impossible size reads as a statement about importance or power that the viewer decodes.
The viewer works out what joining these two meanings is saying.
The shape swap only pays off once the viewer connects the two objects.
The meaning depends on the viewer recognising the borrowed image.
Visible marks signal handmade, honest or raw, which viewers read from what they know about how art is made.
Being left out of a group is a reason to stand out; the lever is how things group.
Eye contact from a person in the picture is a social signal that beats almost everything else for attention.
What a thing is, in the wrong setting, is what makes it stand out; the lever is meaning, not looks.
Shared colour across the whole frame binds unrelated parts into one picture.
A near shape at the edge sends the eye inward and back, so it sets the path through depth.
Arrows and numbers work only because viewers have learned what they mean, so the order comes from shared convention.
The group sets up an expectation, and the gap in it is what the viewer has to explain.
